cards.title: Treat Leaky Abstractions as Likely Edge-Case Holes in Store Code
cards.summary: An abstraction that hides HTTP method details still forces developers to know them, so unmapped methods like HEAD slip through as unhandled cases.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or building shared ecommerce code (library, middleware, internal SDK) that wraps HTTP requests between storefront, checkout, fulfillment or third-party integrations.
steps: Map every case the abstraction claims to handle versus every case the underlying layer can actually deliver. The source's example: the abstraction was written for GET and POST, but HEAD requests still reached the developer's code, which had no case for them and was never told to write one.

Before releasing a wrapper, enumerate all possible inputs (HTTP methods, parameter types, content types) and confirm each has an explicit branch or an explicit rejection — not an implicit fall-through.
Treat any abstraction with many edge cases as 'leaky' and prefer exposing the essential cases explicitly rather than one clever catch-all that mostly works.
If you cannot avoid a leaky wrapper (e.g., a framework's middleware signature), document the hidden requirement loudly in the wrapper so callers don't silently drop it.
caveats: The source presents this as experience-based taste, not a hard rule; everything here is framed as a trade-off, so apply judgment to each wrapper rather than banning abstraction outright.
The $25K loss mentioned is an illustrative anecdote, not a benchmark you can rely on.

cards.title: Reduce Component Interactions, Not Just Component Count
cards.summary: Security risk grows with how many things a new component can interact with, not just how many components you add.
cards.use_when: Scoping a new storefront integration, payment provider connection, fulfillment hook, or automation connector before adding it to the ecommerce stack.
steps: For each proposed addition, ask 'how many existing components can this interact with?' rather than 'how many components am I adding?'
If a new store component or third-party integration could reach 500 other services (e.g., a generic webhook or admin API key with broad scope), treat the change as high-risk and isolate it.
Design the addition so it talks to as few things as possible — e.g., scope a fulfillment or inventory integration to only the endpoints it needs, so a compromise has a limited blast radius.
Count interaction paths, not surface area: 1 component touching 1 is far less scary than 1 touching everything.
caveats: The '500 components' figure is the source's illustrative example, not a measured threshold.

cards.title: Use Explicit Code Over Clever Code in Security-Relevant Paths
cards.summary: Verbose, dumb-looking code you can still understand months later is safer than a clever one-liner no one can audit.
cards.use_when: Writing or reviewing checkout, auth, payment or PII-handling code where future maintainers must be able to verify behavior.
steps: Unroll clever one-liners into plain sequential steps (do this, then this, then this) so the flow is auditable, even if it looks uglier.
Prefer obvious control flow over packed functionality; the source notes that writing less clever code tends to happen as engineers are bitten by clever code they can't re-read a month later.
Treat 'hard to understand' as a defect in any code path that touches money, credentials or user data, because obscurity is not security.
Do not rely on making code hard to read as a defense — the source explicitly rejects security through obscurity.
caveats: The source treats this as career-acquired taste and a trade-off, not a universal coding mandate.

cards.title: Fail Early on Unexpected State; Handle Expected Errors Gracefully
cards.summary: Crash on exceptions you didn't anticipate, but return normal error responses for errors your code explicitly expects.
cards.use_when: Deciding how a store's server should behave when errors occur — e.g., product lookups, cart operations, payment callbacks.
steps: Distinguish expected from unexpected errors. Example from the source: a user-typed URL for a nonexistent user ID is an expected failure — return a 404 and keep the server running.

For unexpected exceptions (e.g., an uncaught exception in the middle of a multi-step process), do not just log and continue; the source argues you can't know what state you left behind and what cleanup was skipped.
Let the process crash and be restarted by a supervisor, and run multiple instances so crashes don't cause user-visible downtime.
Verify your server actually restarts on crash (process manager or orchestrator) before relying on this pattern.
caveats: The source explicitly refines its own earlier advice: crashing is for unexpected errors, not for expected, handled ones like a missing resource.

cards.title: Assume Inputs Are Wrong: Verify Assumptions at the Top of Each Function
cards.summary: Code defensively by validating function arguments and request data up front rather than assuming they match what you expect.
cards.use_when: Building any store endpoint or handler — product search, discount application, admin actions — that trusts request parameters.
steps: Do not assume a function is called with the correct arguments; validate the arguments and the request payload at the start of the handler.
Validate type and shape explicitly. In the source demo, the handler checked that a required field existed and that a type field was one of a small allowed set before proceeding.
After validation, the rest of the handler can proceed on the assumption that inputs are in the expected state (fail fast, then continue confidently).
For security-relevant values (IDs, amounts, resource names), verify the assumption rather than trusting caller-provided types.
caveats: Defensive validation reduces but does not remove risk; the source presents it as one of several trade-off-based lessons, not a guarantee.

cards.title: Reject APIs Whose Insecure Path Is the Easy Path
cards.summary: If a function only works securely when you pass a pile of options, most callers will be insecure by default.
cards.use_when: Choosing or wrapping third-party libraries and SDKs for a store — payment processors, auth providers, encryption helpers, bot-defense tools.
steps: Check the defaults: does calling the function with no options produce secure, sensible behavior? If not, treat it as a footgun.
If you must use it, wrap it in your own function whose defaults are secure, so store developers can't accidentally invoke the unsafe path.

Also flag polymorphic signatures — functions that do different things based on argument type or count — as harder to use correctly, especially in loosely typed languages, and prefer explicit alternatives where available.
caveats: The source presents this as an opinion about good design, not a universal rule; some widely used libraries (jQuery, Node buffers, Express middleware) violate it, so any workaround must be tested against the specific version.

cards.title: Watch for Hidden Behavioral Switches in Function Signatures
cards.summary: Some frameworks change a function's entire behavior based on argument count, so an 'unused' argument can be load-bearing.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or refactoring middleware, hooks or plugin functions in a store's web framework where behavior depends on signature shape.
steps: Treat argument count as part of the contract in frameworks that use it. The source's example: an Express middleware becomes error-handling middleware specifically when it takes four arguments, including an otherwise-unused error parameter.
Do not delete 'unused' parameters during cleanup — removing them can silently change a handler from error-handling to a normal middleware, breaking error flow.
When adding middleware (e.g., CSRF token validation on POST), confirm exactly how the framework routes requests through it and which signature triggers which path.
Verify behavior against the framework's current documentation, since this interface can change between versions.
caveats: Express's behavior is described as of the source's version; verify the current interface before relying on the exact argument-count rule.

cards.title: Secure Binary/Buffer Encoding Endpoints Against Memory Disclosure
cards.summary: Constructing a buffer from a numeric input can allocate uninitialized memory and return stale process data, including secrets.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing any store endpoint that handles binary data, encoding/conversion, or user-supplied buffer-like inputs.
steps: Do not build buffers from unvalidated user input where a number could be mistaken for a size. The source demo: passing a JSON number instead of a string caused the process to allocate memory that was never zeroed, and the response contained leftover process memory, potentially including credentials.
Validate the type and length of encoding inputs explicitly (e.g., allow only string data of bounded length for hex/base64 conversion) and reject unexpected types.
Prefer current, non-deprecated buffer/typed-array APIs and verify their initialization behavior against current documentation; when in doubt, zero or explicitly fill the buffer.
Treat this class of bug as a memory-disclosure risk — the source notes it resembles Heartbleed-style leaks, where repeated requests can eventually expose a server's TLS key.
caveats: The source's demo used a then-current Node Buffer constructor; the specific API may be deprecated now, so confirm against the current runtime.
Everything here must be validated only on systems you own and are authorized to test.

cards.title: Never Bind Servers to All Interfaces by Default
cards.summary: A listen call without an explicit address can expose the service to every machine that can reach the host.
cards.use_when: Deploying or configuring any store service — API, admin panel, internal tool — where bind address and exposure matter.
steps: Check every server start: if you omit an address/host argument, the service may listen on all interfaces, meaning anyone who can reach the host's IP can connect.
For local-only or private services, bind explicitly to localhost/loopback.
For public services, restrict which interfaces are exposed and combine with network controls (firewall, private subnet, auth) rather than relying on the bind address alone.
Confirm the current bind and default behavior of your framework and platform, since defaults differ across languages and hosting environments.
caveats: The source notes the unsafe default surprised it; the specific default depends on runtime and version, so always verify.

cards.title: Add CSRF Validation Centrally for State-Changing Requests
cards.summary: Route-wide middleware that checks CSRF tokens on state-changing methods is the pattern the source cites for validating requests globally.
cards.use_when: Securing store forms and state-changing endpoints — checkout submission, cart mutation, account changes, admin actions.
steps: Implement a middleware that runs before every request and validates a CSRF token when the request is a state-changing method (e.g., POST).
Apply it globally rather than per-route so no new endpoint forgets the check.
Use the same layer for other cross-cutting checks (logging, token verification) and only pass the request onward when valid.
Verify current framework guidance on token issuance, SameSite cookies and rotation, since these mechanisms evolve.
caveats: The source mentions CSRF in passing as an example; it does not provide a complete CSRF implementation, and CSRF protection is one layer and not a full defense.

cards.title: Use Strongly Typed Checks to Force Exhaustive Case Handling
cards.summary: A compiler that errors on unhandled cases prevents the class of bug where a developer handles only some input variants.
cards.use_when: Choosing languages or tooling for store components that branch on request type, payment status or order state where missing a case is costly.
steps: Where the risk of an unhandled case is high (e.g., payment callbacks with many statuses), consider a strongly typed language that produces a compile-time error if a case is missed.
Weigh the trade-off: the source acknowledges stronger typing can slow development and teams often choose loosely typed languages deliberately.
If you stay in a loosely typed language, compensate with explicit runtime validation and tests covering each branch instead of clever introspection.
Avoid hacky runtime introspection of source code (e.g., parsing a function's string form to check handling) — the source explicitly does not recommend it.
caveats: The source frames strong typing as one possible mitigation and a trade-off, not a required choice.
